title: Who was Cain's wife? (Genesis 4:16–5:27)
hookLine: the questions kids ask about Genesis: who Cain married, nine-hundred-year lives, and where the dinosaurs went

cards: A Sunday school classroom: a felt board, juice boxes, a teacher who has just finished Cain and Abel. One brother killed, the other sent away. And a seven-year-old's hand goes up.
But who did Cain marry? Weren't they the only people? The teacher smiles, a little stuck.
Kids ask the best questions about Genesis. Who did Cain marry? Did people really live nine hundred years?
Where are the dinosaurs? They often get waved away, and that's a shame, because they're good questions.

teach.b: Genesis says, in the King James Bible: "And Cain went out from the presence of the LORD, and dwelt in the land of Nod, on the east of Eden. And Cain knew his wife." That's all.
Nod is Hebrew for wandering, so the wanderer settles in Wander-land. Then a wife, a son, and a city. Readers have answered the puzzle in two main ways.
The oldest: Adam and Eve had more children.
The next chapter says Adam "begat sons and daughters." So Cain married a sister. An ancient Jewish book, Jubilees, even names her: Awan.
Augustine agreed that at the very start it had to be so. Other readers notice that Cain fears "every one that findeth me shall slay me," and then builds a city. Who is everyone?
They read Genesis as a story of beginnings, not a census, so other people are simply there in the background.
The long lives get read in more than one way too: "all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty and nine years." Some take the numbers literally.
Others note that ancient lists from Mesopotamia give their early kings reigns of thousands of years, and hear Genesis speaking in that style. And dinosaurs? The Bible never mentions them.
Many churches, Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant, see no conflict with a very old earth; others read the days of creation literally.

And tucked into that same family tree, one man gets a single quiet line: "Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him." Genesis keeps its mysteries short, and leaves room for the questions.

how: Christians answer questions like Cain's wife in different ways: many follow the old view that Adam and Eve had other children, and others read Genesis as a story of beginnings that doesn't name everyone. Churches differ on reading the ages and the days of creation literally.

games.q: you're the Sunday school teacher. a seven-year-old asks: who did Cain marry? what do you do?
o: tell them not to ask silly questions.
say it's a good question, and share how people have answered it.
games.why: readers have taken it seriously for centuries: Jubilees named her, Augustine reasoned it through. the question was a good one.

practice: Bring back one question about the Bible, or about faith, that you once asked and got waved away, or never asked at all, and say it to yourself plainly without answering it.
Let it sit in the room, the way Genesis lets its mysteries sit. If you pray, you can bring it to God as a question, not a test; if you don't, simply notice that asking it didn't break anything.

wordCard.voice: Nod. Hebrew for wandering: the land east of Eden where Cain settled, married and built a city.

orig.note: Hebrew: wandering. the land of Nod, east of Eden (Genesis 4:16), where the wanderer settles.
